title: Wearing the 'Eat at Joe's' Sign
text:
In 1977 Lee Ross, David Greene and Pamela House of Stanford University asked students a strange favor. Would they walk around campus for thirty minutes wearing a large sandwich board sign that read "Eat at Joe's"? Students were told they could learn something useful from the experience, but that they were free to refuse.

Some agreed and some refused. Then each was asked to estimate how many other students would make the same choice, and to describe the kind of person who would agree or refuse. Those who agreed to wear the sign estimated that most of their peers would also agree, on average around 60 percent. Those who refused estimated that only about a third would agree. Each group saw its own choice as the common and sensible one.

The students also judged people who would make the opposite choice more harshly, describing them in more extreme terms and attributing their choice to their personality. Ross and his colleagues found the same pattern with questionnaires about many other preferences and opinions. They called it the false consensus effect: we tend to believe our own choices and views are more widely shared than they are, and to see those who differ as odd.
lesson: Others are less like you than you assume. When someone makes a choice you would not, ask what they see before deciding something is wrong with them.
people: Lee Ross, David Greene, Pamela House
source: Ross, L., Greene, D., and House, P. (1977). The 'false consensus effect': An egocentric bias in social perception and attribution processes. Journal of Experimental Social Psychology, 13(3), 279-301.
